title: Day 2 - Babies A, B, & C
section: Lucy Letby - Cross-examination by Nick Johnson KC

blocks.text: Lucy Letby - Cross-examination Day 2: Babies A, B & C
MS LUCY LETBY (continued)
Cross-examination by MR JOHNSON (continued)
Thursday, 18 May 2023
(In the presence of the jury)
MS LUCY LETBY (continued)
Cross-examination by MR JOHNSON (continued)

Ms Letby, yesterday you answered several questions from me on several issues. Is there anything that you said during the course of my questioning to you that you have thought about overnight and you want to modify any of the answers that you have given?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: One of the statements of fact that you made to the jury was that student nurses are not given handover sheets.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Was that true?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When you were a student nurse, were you given any handover sheets?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sometimes, yes, but the neonatal unit didn't tend to give them out to students at that point.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Could just repeat that answer because I'm not quite sure I understood it.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What do you mean? As a student nurse, yes, I had handover sheets from certain areas, but routinely the neonatal unit at the Countess at that time did not provide students with a handover.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I just want to understand this answer: when you were a student at the Countess of Chester Hospital, were you given handover sheets?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At some placements, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Some placements? Do you mean in different parts of the hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, all I'm interested in is the neonatal unit, so if you would concentrate on that. Were you given handover sheets from the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't recall specifically.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You know where I'm going, don't you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Pause)
Do you know where Mr Johnson's going? No?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She shook her head. She doesn't know where you're going.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Did you have any handover sheets at your house from when you were a student at the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I couldn't say. I've got handover sheets, I don't know where they're from.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Is that true?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What was the first day that you worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital in the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: 2 January 2012.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: As a student?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When I was a student? I don't recall the date. It would have been between 2008 and 2011, I can't recall specifically what dates all my placements were.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm going to suggest to you that the first day you worked on the neonatal unit as a student was 1 June 2010.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And the reason I'm making that suggestion to you is that there is a handover sheet in your house -- or was a handover sheet in your house from that date?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Are you agreeing with me?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. At the time that we're talking about, students did not have handover sheets.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why didn't you say that when I asked you the question a few minutes ago, that we did get handover sheets when I was a student but the students no longer get handover sheets?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I believe I did say at the time that the practice now is that they do not have a handover sheet.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Are you doing your best to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Where was that handover sheet dated 1 June 2010?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have no idea.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you have a keepsake box with roses on it in your house at 41 Westbourne Road?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What was in the keepsake box?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't recall from memory.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: One of the things in the keepsake box was that handover sheet, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't know. I don't have any recollection of where the handover sheets were.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm going to show it to you as the police recovered it, please. It's exhibit WG3.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just have a look at that, if you would. Is that from your house?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't say. I don't recall this specific individual handover sheet, no.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Just take it in your hands. What's unusual about it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Pick it up. What's unusual about it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't know what you mean. It's a standard handover sheet.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: It is. But how does it differ from all the other handover sheets that you took home?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It hasn't got handwriting on it.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: That's one difference. Another is it hasn't got any folds in it either, has it? It's in pristine condition.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is this the original?
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: It is the original. In the keepsake box in your house.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, let's just be clear. Do you agree it hasn't got any folds in it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I agree, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: All right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You knew where you were keeping these handover sheets, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. They were in several locations, I believe, throughout the property.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: They were. And there were 99 handover sheets from your time as a student, weren't there, in your house?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't comment on that, I don't know how many there were.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Does that sound about right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I wouldn't know. I don't know how many handover sheets I had in different locations until I've been told now how many there were in total.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You are not, and you have not been prepared to tell the truth about these handover sheets, have you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The truth is what I've told you.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: May I formally exhibit that handover sheet, please, my Lord?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I want to deal with a bit of evidence that you gave yesterday on the subject of handover sheets. If Mr Murphy would help me, please, by opening up on the screens tile 331 in the [Baby O] sequence, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you remember giving us some evidence about this yesterday?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And your explanation, I'm going to suggest, and I'd ask you either to agree or disagree, was that you took the handover sheet for 23 June home and the reason that you took it home was because on the back of it you had written down details of drugs that had been given to [Baby O] or another child that you were looking after that day. Am I right so far?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was documentation on there. I'm not sure exactly what was on there, but yes, the handover sheet did have writing on it, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, I'll remind you of exactly what you said, seeing as we don't seem to be going in the same direction. You said to Mr Myers:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "It's common practice that we will utilise the handover sheets. So we would write on the back of the handover sheet and if something significant happens, we would just grab the nearest available paper or paper towel, something to write on so that we can then document retrospectively."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then Mr Myers asked you this question:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "When in this note [and he's referring at this point, Mr Myers, to what we can see on the screen] you finish, 'Left off signing for drugs until tomorrow', can you explain to us what that refers to?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And you said:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "So I hadn't completed all of the documentation for the medications."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So "for the medications", concentrate on those words, please:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "And as I was back in work the next day, I planned to do it then."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You were then asked this question:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "What was happening with whatever notes you had in between the end of your shift and completing writing up medications the next day?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So do you agree with me that the essence of the questions and answers is that this is all to do with medications?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Medication was included, yes. I don't know that it's medications in its entirety.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And you said:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I needed it for the next day."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You were then asked the question:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "So where was it?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Talking about the note. And you said:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "It came back."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In other words, you took it back home. That's what you meant, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I took it to bring it back into work the next day, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Where was it?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Said Mr Myers. And you said:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "At this point in my pocket."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And you confirmed that the notes were in your pocket.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then there was a bit of confusion between the two of you and Mr Myers said:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Probably my fault. You've got the notes in your pocket. You've said something about 'left signing up drugs until tomorrow', which we can see on the screen. You're talking about walking home. What's going to happen to those bits of paper?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And you then said:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "They're going to come back to work the next day."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: By that, you meant you were going to take them into work the next day, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes. And Mr Myers said:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Question: 23 June, you have the handover sheet, which includes on it [Baby P] and [Baby O] --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Answer: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Question: -- and the various notes on the back of that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Answer: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Question: Is that the handover sheet that you would have taken home with you at the end of the shift, if you remember?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Answer: Yes. So that's the exchange between you. There, you were saying that you needed -- you took the handover sheet home deliberately; do you accept that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: The reason for taking it home deliberately was because you needed it for the next day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And the reason you needed it for the next day was because you hadn't completed writing up the medications and you needed the notes on the back of the handover sheet to remind you of what you needed to write the next day; do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Or for any other documentation that still needed to be completed.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: No, no. The question and the answers were very specific: it was all to do with medications, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, here, yes, I'm referring to drugs, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes. And the question and answers between you and Mr Myers were referring to drugs, weren't they?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, if that's what it said, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. I'm going to show you the handover sheet, the original handover sheet. Just for the record, what I'm about to hand over is exhibit 15, which has already been exhibited in the trial. It is, just in case these documents get separated, four
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: handover sheets that were in the Ibiza bag: 23 June, 24 June, 25 June and 28 June.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So they're all on a paper clip at the moment with a court sticker on the front sheet.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Handed)
What I'd like to do also is give the jury photocopies. I'd invite people to put this behind divider 10 in jury bundle 1.
I'm going to ask Mr Stansfield to give you a copy of what the jury have, which is a redacted or edited copy.

I'm going to ask you to confirm, if you would -- could you take the original, the first sheet of the originals out from the -that's it. Would you compare, and take as much time as you like, the original to the copy that we've just given to the jury, a version of which you have as well? And would you confirm that it is the same document, apart from the fact that the names of the children other than "Male [Surname of Baby Q]", who we know is [Baby Q], and [Baby P] and [Baby O], have all been edited out?
Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Would you now turn over the original and compare it to the second page that I have just handed you as a copy?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it's the same.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: The same document. Right. I'm not interested in the front of this document for these purposes. I'm interested in the back and your notes. You point out to us where the notes of the medications are you have made on the back of that document.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's a note about caffeine and [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. So this is the top left; yes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: "Caffeine" underlined?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right, okay. Anything else for [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: [Baby O]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, the drugs were written on a paper towel, I believe.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: The child whose name has been edited out, who was the third child in nursery 2?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's no medications.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So your evidence to the jury yesterday is that you took that home because it had caffeine written on it and you brought it in the next day to help you remember, what caffeine, is that the thing you're struggling --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I didn't say that, I didn't say I'd taken it because of caffeine.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: No, you said you took it for the drugs.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, with the paper towel that was also with it.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: There's a paper towel with it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, we've seen the paper towel, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, there was a -- there have been a couple of paper towels. I'm interested -- you were answering questions about the handover sheet. That's why I started with reminding you of what your evidence was. Were you telling the truth to the jury yesterday?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: The Morrisons bag. When did that bag go under your bed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't recall a specific date when I would have put that under the bed.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, give us a range of dates if you would, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, the Ibiza bag sort of replaced that bag, so it would be after -- just before that time maybe or after.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So just before -- so some time around the 20-somethingth of June 2016?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't be specific, but the Ibiza bag became my new work bag, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. And in the Morrisons bag there were 31 handover sheets, we've heard, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And they were dated between July 2014 and then April 2015 through to June 2016; do you accept that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Obviously, I can't see it now but if that's been agreed, then yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I can produce the sheets. Would you like to see them?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, if it's been agreed...
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How did all those handover sheets get into that bag?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They didn't get there on their own, did they?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So you tell us the process between emptying out your uniform when you're about to launder it to those handover sheets ending up in that bag, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When I've come home from work and I've taken my uniform off, the contents of the pocket have gone into the work bag.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And where does the work bag then go on the next day, the next work day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: To work.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes. So, what, you're ferrying handover sheets to and from the Countess of Chester, is that what you're saying?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't say definitively.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, that must be what you're saying, mustn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I accept that they're all in that bag, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, they're all in the bag when the police find it.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What I'm more interested in is, first of all, why you put them into that bag at all.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't recall.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Can't or won't?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, I collect -- paper just gathers. They were just bits of paper to me.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You're not telling the truth, are you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I am.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why don't you want to tell the truth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is the truth. They have no meaning to me at all, they're just pieces of paper.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: If they have no meaning to you, why do you keep them?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because I keep a lot of paper, I have difficulty throwing anything away. I have copious amounts of paper, cards, notes throughout my whole life. These are no different: they're just pieces of paper that have been gathered and I've never done anything with them.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, you have: you've put them into different bags in different places.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, as a piece of paper, not because of the content.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I've moved paper round my whole life.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Oh yes, you have, and that's one of the reasons I asked you the questions about where you were living at various points.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I accept possessions came with me to multiple addresses, and that's including these handover sheets as well as many other handwritten things: cards, letters, notes. It's the paper that I accumulate, not the content.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: The question that the jury may be interested in is: why?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have difficulty throwing anything away.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Is that why you bought a shredder?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did have a shredder at some point, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes. That wasn't the question. The question is: is your difficulty in throwing things away the reason why you bought a shredder?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I bought a shredder for certain documents once I bought the house, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. Which documents were going to go in the shredder?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Predominantly bank statements.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why not handover sheets?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I didn't know I had the handover sheets, they were insignificant to me at that time.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: They were in your work bag which was going to and from work every day.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: With lots of other paper as well.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Where's all that other paper gone then?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have various amounts of paper at home of different things --
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: No, no, don't deflect the question.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't know what you mean, sorry.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We're talking about the work bag. Where is all the other paper in the work bag?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm talking about there's multiple handover sheets in there.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes. So they're going to and from work with you every day. Every day when you empty out your uniform, you add to the pile; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I must have done. I can't recall specifically every day what action I took.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, of course not, on an individual basis, but what were you thinking as this pile of handover sheets accumulated to almost the size of a phone book?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They weren't the size of a phone book in one area, I didn't recall that I had that many in different locations.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, don't argue about whether it's a phone book or not. What were you thinking as you were accumulating the handover sheets?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I wasn't thinking anything, they're just bits of paper.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So put them in the shredder.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I didn't shred anything particularly other than bank statements.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When did you buy the shredder?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't recall an exact date that I bought a shredder.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm not asking for the exact date. Did you have it in Ash House?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So you bought it some time between 5 April 2016 and the date that the police knocked on your door?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why didn't you shred the handover sheets?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because they're insignificant. I haven't shredded a lot of documents in my house that could have been shredded.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: These are very significant documents, aren't they, Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, they are sitting here now. They weren't to me at that time. They're just pieces of paper.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: They have the names on dead children on them, don't they?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They have the names of a lot of children on them, yes, and they shouldn't have come home, I agree, but they were in a home with me where nobody else was, they were confidential, they were just put in amongst a lot of other notes and bits of paper, study notes that I've kept my whole life.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Are you really asking the jury to accept that pieces of paper with sensitive information about dead children are insignificant?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'd like to look at [Baby M]'s blood gas document, please, which is in his sequence of events at tile 171.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's also J18905 -- I've got the wrong reference.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Let me give you the original. I've got the wrong reference for the point I want to make. This, my Lord, was produced to the court on 21 February this year.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's exhibits 7 and 8.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: These documents were in your Morrisons bag, weren't they?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Are they insignificant?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At the time of being found, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So a child who brushed with death, these are his blood gas readings taken whilst he was being resuscitated, you regard those as insignificant?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think the context is different. These have come home with me, with many babies, they're not just for babies on the indictment. It's not insensitive, they've just come back as pieces of paper and have ended up just being treated that way, as bits of paper.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: They haven't come home with you, have they? You took them home.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I took them home, yes, but not with any intention.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I will.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you agree that [Baby L] was poisoned with insulin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You've asked me ways that it could happen, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes, I'll be a bit more specific then: knowing what you know about the insulin readings or the blood sugar readings, to be more precise, what are the realistic possibilities in [Baby L]'s case as you see it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't believe that any member of staff on the unit would make a mistake in giving insulin.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: No. Mistake is not an option in this case for the insulin babies, is it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's for [Baby F] as well, for [Baby F] as well, you accept that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So it's deliberate poisoning by someone, but not you?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Insulin has been added by somebody. I can't comment on how or who.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just that it was not me.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What about when?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When what?
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, again, I will come back to this; all right? Let's take [Baby L]. When was the insulin first put in [Baby L]'s dextrose bag?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, I don't know because I didn't put insulin in, so I've no idea.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: But what do the blood sugar results tell us as to when it was put in?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't recall now without looking at the charts.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: All right. Well, I'll come back to that. Park that for now.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Have you not given that any thought as to when it's happened?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, but I haven't got the details in front of me right now.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Okay. I will always give you the opportunity to look at documents, don't worry. Don't feel under any pressure from me to answer any question without looking at the documents if you feel you need to look at them. All right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: But what are the dangers of unprescribed insulin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes, but what's likely to happen if it is given to a patient who doesn't need it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm going to move on to your QIS training; all right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: This is the last subject I'm going to deal with before I turn to [Baby A]. I will deal with the babies in the same order that Mr Myers did to help you. So that's the menu.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't remember now, but if that's agreed then, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: It's what you said on 2 May.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: If anyone wants to check what you said, if they look at page 32 of that transcript, they will find that that is what you said.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think you told the jury that it involved a university module, a placement at the Women's Hospital in Liverpool and it took about 6 months.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And that you couldn't be specific as to the date that you qualified but, as you remembered it, it was March/April of 2014; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I beg your pardon. My mistake.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When you were asked to summarise what the consequence of the qualification was, you said it meant that you were qualified to look after intensive care babies.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Subject, of course, to the point that we've already made about the fact that a child in nursery 1 isn't always intensive care.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And so at the time that you dealt with [Baby A] and [Baby B] at the beginning of June 2015, how long had you been qualified to access the lines of neonates?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And what did you understand from your education and wider knowledge were the dangers of injecting air into a line?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think all nursing staff know that any air getting into a patient could ultimately lead to death.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes. Even in the films, when a doctor is about to give an injection to a patient, you see them tap the syringe and squirt a bit of liquid out at the end, don't you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So everybody knows the dangers of air embolus, don't they, pretty much?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it's part of your nurse training, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: But even people with no medical training like me, everybody knows, don't they?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't speak for everyone.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: All right. Let's start with the case of [Baby A], please. You were first interviewed on 4 July 2018.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Independently of the medical notes, did you have any memory of [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Just for anyone's note, it is, of course, count 1.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was born on 7 June and died a day later on the 8th, and he was, as we all know, the twin of [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Before [Baby A], had you ever known a child to die unexpectedly within about 24 hours of birth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't comment on that. I'm not sure.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, how many infant deaths had you witnessed in your employment before [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Not many, maybe two or three at the Countess and then several more on my placements at Liverpool Women's.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Two more at Liverpool Women's? You say several more.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm offering an alternative of two more.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't say. I don't keep track of numbers.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm just going off what you said to the police, you see.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, my memory then would have been clearer than it is now.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Okay. Well, we can go to the interviews if you'd like to check it, page 16 of your [Baby A] interview.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm suggesting that you told the police that you'd seen two at Liverpool.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Does that sound right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When [Baby A] and [Baby B] were born, were the staff, including the nursing staff, talking about their mother's antiphospholipid syndrome?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Not at the time -- when I was looking after [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: At any time. You tell us.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, the first time I met [Baby A] and was on shift was the day of the event. Afterwards, the condition was talked about, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Was it being offered up as an explanation for what had happened as far as you were aware?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was possibly a contributing factor. That was what was being discussed at the time.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: But we now know that it wasn't, don't we?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Is it your case that the staffing levels in the Countess of Chester Hospital contributed to [Baby A]'s death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In part, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. How?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Through the amount of time that he was without fluids for and the issues around the lines' insertion.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. So he was without fluids from some time about 4 pm or thereabouts, 3 or 4 pm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So your case is, what, that he died from dehydration?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. I'm saying they're contributing factors.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: But according to you, at least, how did that lack of fluids for about 4 hours contribute to his death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What's your case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That it would have put him at increased risk of collapse and he would have had less reserves to then fight off any infection or any procedures that we were doing.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So it's your case that 4 hours without fluids killed [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, that's not what I'm saying, no.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't tell you how [Baby A] died. I don't know --
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- but they're contributing factors that were missed.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Is it your case that the competence of the medical staff contributed to [Baby A]'s death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, I can't say definitively how [Baby A] died but, yes, I think the issues around his lines made his more vulnerable, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And what issue around his lines made him more vulnerable?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That he was left with a line in situ, a UVC, that was not for use and was due to be removed and it wasn't.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And then having a long line sited and time passing by without that line being connected to anything and being confirmed on Xray. It's not usual practice.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: All right. Did you fill in a Datix?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why not?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I just haven't.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You fill in lots of Datix forms, don't you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Three at the end of June 2016.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We'll come to them, but two of which contained lies, according to Dr Brearey; yes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: According to Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes. If you seriously thought that [Baby A]'s death was contributed to by him not having fluids for any significant period of time, why didn't you fill in a Datix form?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was discussed amongst staff, we all talked about that as contributing factors at the time. That was readily discussed amongst staff, including the consultant.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: No, no, the question is, why did you --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I didn't feel I needed to do a Datix. It had been raised verbally by senior staff -- to senior staff.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And those senior staff were who?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Ravi Jayaram and other members of the nursing team.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: No, Ravi Jayaram and?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I didn't say two senior staff: I escalated the concerns to senior staff --
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Oh, I beg your pardon.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- one being Ravi Jayaram, the other senior nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood what you said, I apologise.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And part of that discussion is why we then kept the fluids and the line from [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'll come to that in a moment, if I may. Was [Baby A]'s death anything to do with Mel Taylor?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't know why [Baby A] died.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: But I'm asking you whether it's your case that it had anything to do with Mel Taylor.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we agree that the cause of death was an air embolus then I believe she attached fluids to those lines, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So that's Mel Taylor's fault?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, if that's what we agree, that [Baby A] has died from that, then yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Because you weren't standing over him at the time he collapsed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, I did not have any access to his lines, so therefore if an embolism came, it must have come from the person connecting the fluids, which is not me.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Would you admit it if you did?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did what?
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Put air into him.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I haven't put air in so I am not going to --
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: The question is: would you admit it if you did?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's not something I would ever do.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you about some of the descriptions that have been given by your colleagues in evidence about [Baby A] to see whether you agree or disagree with them.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Starting with Dr Beech's evidence. On 7 June, Dr Beech told the jury that [Baby A] was doing well, that he was crying and vigorous on stimulation shortly after his birth at about 9 pm, 21.00 hours, on 7 June. Do you disagree with that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, I wasn't present for that, so...
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: The following day, the day he died, which was Monday, 8 June, at 09.45 Dr Ogden, at tile 84, described [Baby A] as "handling well". Do you disagree with that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, I wasn't there so I can't comment. That's her opinion.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, are you aware of anything to contradict --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: -- Dr Ogden's opinion?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And as you've already told us, in the afternoon there were problems identified with the UVC and then the cannula to which he was attached became blocked?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you remember that at 19.00 hours on 8 June, Dr Harkness put a central line into [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I know that happened, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you accept that you were standing over [Baby A] at the time he collapsed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I accept that I was within his cot space checking equipment, yes.

blocks.text: How close were you to him at the time he collapsed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was in the close vicinity, I was checking the equipment around his incubator.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes, give us an idea in terms of this court. Could you reach out and touch him?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I could touch the incubator, not -- I'd have to open the doors to actually get into the baby, but yes I could touch the outside of the incubator.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Could you touch the lines?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why not?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The incubator was closed.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you accept that at the time [Baby A] collapsed, Mel Taylor was on the computer doing her nursing notes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: It's your case, and correct me if I have misunderstood, that Mel Taylor was the sterile nurse in terms of attaching [Baby A]'s line.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you accept that it was at 20.05 hours that the bag was hung?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you accept that you co-signed for that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And do you accept that the order of the signatures doesn't illuminate the question of who it was that actually hung --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, there's no way of knowing from signatures.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: It was 15 minutes later, wasn't it, that [Baby A] collapsed at 20.20?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And what I'm going to do is to remind you of various people's descriptions of what they saw. Okay? What I'm going to ask you is whether you agree or disagree with their descriptions.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you understand?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So if you want me to repeat any of this, you say so; all right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm quoting from the transcript and I'm going to start with Dr Harkness. For your Lordship's note, this is Day 12, pages 90 to 92.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: What Dr Harkness said was this:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "There was a very unusual patchiness of the skin, which I had never seen before and I have only seen in cases since within the Countess of Chester Hospital and nothing other than that."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm not asking you to comment on what he has or hasn't -- what he says about having seen things, but do you agree with his description that there was a very unusual patchiness of his skin?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.

blocks.text: "There were patches of a kind of blue/purple colour, there were patches of bright red colour, there were white patches and they didn't fit with something that you would find on a baby that's not pumping any blood around their body."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: "This had bright red patches, which does not fit because red patches means you've got blood going round your body."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: "It had purple patches, it had white patches."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I agree with that, yes, he had mottling.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: No red marks?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: No red blotchiness?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sitting here now, I can't recall any blotchiness, no.

blocks.text: Are you saying Dr Harkness has made that up?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I didn't see it. If he saw something that I didn't, that's something he has to justify.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's not something I saw.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. Well, I'm not interested in, at the moment -- I will come to what you saw. The question is: are you disputing what Dr Harkness says he saw?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because I was present and I did not see those.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. So because you didn't see it, you are disputing it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Are you suggesting he's lying about it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That isn't a proper question, in my submission, to ask if they're lying in that situation.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's been put to the witnesses that they are lying. I want to know what the defendant's case is.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think that the point -- what the witness has said is that description that is given by Dr Harkness does not accord with what she saw.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.

My Lord, there is a matter that arises that I'd like to raise now because I see the way in which certain topics are being dealt with by the prosecution and if the concern I raise is correct, I'd rather raise it now than wait. It's to deal with the form of questioning in cross-examination. I'm assisted by the commentary in Archbold that deals with this, which is at section 8-258 if your Lordship wishes to look at that --

blocks.text: I think I know what you're going to say about putting -- inviting a witness to comment on the evidence of another witness.

blocks.text: Yes, because what's actually happening is, under the guise of reminding the witness or the jury of another witness's evidence, what we're actually having is rehearsal of their evidence and then the defendant really being invited to comment upon it and extended questioning upon that, which, in my submission, goes well beyond what's acceptable with it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We do object to that. It's one thing for a witness to be prompted and, in a long trial, for the jury to be assisted by having attention drawn to something that was said. And then asking what the witness in this case, the defendant, says in response. But to then persistently go beyond that and asking, "Well, what do you say they say that for", or, "Are they telling the truth", or, "Are all these people wrong", questioning like that. We're quite plainly going into territory that is a matter of argument, really, and going well beyond the form of questioning for cross-examination.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I did try to give Mr Johnson a steer in relation to what I consider might be an appropriate question in relation to this. Mr Johnson, do you wish to say anything about this?
